findings.title: PowerShell and PowerShell Remoting processes opened LSASS with full memory-read access on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z and 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16.654Z — full access masks that include 'Read from process memory', the classic LSASS-dump signature. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the PowerShell Remoting host) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF at 03:09:29.430Z, and its CallTrace shows the PowerShell Commands.Management native image, indicating a PowerShell-based tool performing the access. Windows Security 4656 on scranton shows the pbeesly account via powershell.exe requesting AccessMask 0x1F3FFF on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. This is consistent with an adversary dumping LSASS memory for credential theft.

findings.title: LSASS wrote cached domain credential entry HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 728) set the registry value HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 (Details: Binary Data) repeatedly between 2020-05-02T03:11:40Z and 03:15:03Z. The SECURITY\Cache\NL$ keys hold cached domain credentials (DCC/DCC2 hashes). While lsass legitimately updates this key on interactive logon, the repeated writes clustered in the same window as the LSASS memory access on the same host are consistent with cached-credential manipulation/access activity.

findings.title: SAM object handle requests on scranton were made by lsass itself (benign system behaviour)
findings.summary: Windows Security 4656 events on scranton.dmevals.local show handle requests to Security Account Manager objects (SAM_SERVER 'SAM', SAM_DOMAIN 'SCRANTON', SAM_ALIAS 'DOMAINS\Builtin\Aliases\00000221'). In every case the requesting process is C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe running as the machine account (SCRANTON$, S-1-5-18), which is normal LSA/SAM operation, not an external tool reading the SAM hive. No reg save / hive-copy activity against SAM was observed (checks C019/C020/C024 returned zero hits).

findings.title: Adversary credential-access tooling on scranton (pbeesly) — exfil staging script and LSASS access
findings.summary: The pbeesly account on scranton.dmevals.local ran a PowerShell script block 'Invoke-Exfil' (ScriptBlock ID b2b03a9c-43f0-4285-837d-f22d4600b2ae, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1) that compresses user files with a password and copies them to a WebDAV share at \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!). The same account's PowerShell activity includes file-collection targeting *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn* files. Combined with the LSASS full-access opens by PowerShell on the same host, this is consistent with an adversary performing credential access and collection.

findings.title: Azure Network Watcher agent performs netsh packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: The only packet-capture activity in the window is the legitimate Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent. On scranton.dmevals.local, NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (running as SYSTEM, parent services.exe) launched netsh.exe to start a capture to an .etl file under C:\windows\TEMP, then stopped it ~7s later. The same agent also ran Install/Test/Start /service /autoStart and logman trace create/start/stop for Azure guest-agent ETW sessions. This is standard Azure VM network diagnostics, not adversary sniffing.

findings.title: No sniffing tools or capture drivers found on any host
findings.summary: Searches for classic sniffing tooling came back empty: no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap process creation in sysmon event 1, no pcap/npcap/winpcap/ndis/netmon driver image loads in sysmon event 6, no pcap/sniff/promiscuous command lines in security 4688 or PowerShell 4104, and no ICMP conn records in zeek. The 7045 service installations observed (Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service / javamtsup.exe on scranton, PSEXESVC on nashua) are not capture drivers. No evidence of network sniffing by an adversary.

findings.title: Adjacent credential-access activity (PsExec with cleartext password, sdelete) is not network sniffing
findings.summary: While hunting T1040 I observed unrelated but notable activity on scranton.dmevals.local: user pbeesly ran PsExec64.exe from SysinternalsSuite against \\NASHUA passing the cleartext password Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by, spawning C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua via PSEXESVC (repeated ~4x), and ran sdelete64.exe to wipe files including C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr. This is credential/lateral-movement activity, not packet sniffing, so it does not satisfy T1040; recorded here for context only.

On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 3876, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z — full process access including read/write memory and duplicate-handle rights, the classic signature of credential API hooking / LSASS memory access. The matching Security 4656 event shows pbeesly's powershell requesting AccessMask 0x1F3FFF on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. This is not the benign 0x1000 query-information access seen from svchost.exe.
findings.title: PowerShell opens LSASS with full-access rights (0x1fffff / 0x1f3fff) on scranton

findings.summary: At 2020-05-02T03:21:29Z on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed an obfuscated PowerShell script block (function 'jzI' with random parameter names) that resolves Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods and calls GetProcAddress via reflection — a technique used to dynamically resolve and invoke native APIs (e.g. for hooking/credential access) while evading static detection. The same session also ran a gzip+base64 encoded scriptblock launched via a hidden powershell process, and 'Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas' for elevation.
findings.title: Obfuscated PowerShell using GetProcAddress / UnsafeNativeMethods on scranton

findings.summary: The bulk of LSASS process-access events are benign: svchost.exe opened lsass.exe 286 times with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION), and Azure agents (AntimalwareConfig.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe) used 0x1400. Security 4656 events show lsass.exe itself and MsMpEng.exe (Windows Defender) requesting handles to lsass.exe, and CollectGuestLogs.exe — all normal system/AV behaviour, not credential theft.
findings.title: Benign LSASS handle access by system processes (svchost, Defender, Azure agents)

findings.summary: No Sysmon process-creation or PowerShell script-block events contained keylogger indicators (keylog, GetAsyncKeyState, SetWindowsHookEx) — the corresponding checks returned zero hits. The only process-access targets were standard system processes; no evidence of keystroke interception was found.
findings.title: No keylogging artifacts observed

findings.summary: Checks for credential-prompt abuse (Credential/prompt/Read-Host in script blocks and process command lines) returned no hits. The only 'prompt' string seen was a bare PowerShell token in pbeesly's session, not a credential-prompt capture. No GUI input capture activity identified.
findings.title: No GUI input capture / credential prompt abuse observed

findings.summary: Checks for web-portal credential capture (IIS/wwwroot/inetpub file writes, w3wp/iis process creation, login/portal URLs in Zeek HTTP) returned zero hits across sysmon, security, powershell and zeek datasets. No evidence of web portal capture.
findings.title: No web portal capture observed
No brute-force authentication activity; credential theft occurred via LSASS access instead
findings.summary: Across windows.security (41002 events, 02:55-03:28Z), windows.other, windows.powershell and windows.sysmon there are zero failed-logon events (event.code 4625) and no lockout or spray tooling. The only authentication-related hits are benign: a Remote Desktop session logon succeeded for DMEVALS\pbeesly on scranton (event.code 21), a Customer Experience Improvement Program logon notification (7001), and normal explicit-credential logons (4648) from winlogon/wininit/taskhostw and PSEXESVC. No brute-force pattern (repeated failures, many usernames, many source IPs) exists in the data.

findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by steganographic PowerShell payload on scranton

The same process (SourceProcessId 2976) then opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff at 03:05:16Z — the classic signature of in-memory credential dumping (e.g. MiniDumpWriteDump) to obtain password hashes for offline cracking. A separate 4104 script block on scranton defines Invoke-Exfil, which compresses the user's Downloads with a password and copies the archive to a WebDAV share at \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!). This is attacker credential-access tooling, not brute force.

findings.title: No password-spraying pattern observed
findings.summary: No 4625 failures exist to indicate spraying, and the 4648 explicit-credential logons are all legitimate: repeated PSEXESVC.exe logons on nashua using pbeesly credentials (remote admin), and winlogon/wininit/taskhostw machine-account logons on scranton. The only command line referencing 'user' is userinit.exe. No single-source, many-account authentication attempts were found.

findings.title: No credential-stuffing activity observed
findings.summary: No failed logons (4625) and no credential-list-driven authentication attempts were found. The credential-related windows.other messages are benign system events (Credential Guard configuration 0x0, a SAM remote-call security descriptor notice, and the RDP logon success). The credential material seen in the environment (hardcoded cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd! in the Invoke-Exfil script) is used for outbound WebDAV exfiltration, not for stuffing against accounts.

findings.title: Explicit-credential logons (4648) for pbeesly via PsExec — lateral movement, not MFA interception
findings.summary: On 2020-05-01/02, 15 event.code 4648 'logon using explicit credentials' events occurred. 9 used the account pbeesly, executed by C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local and C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local, targeting localhost. These are PsExec-style remote execution artifacts (PSEXESVC service installs, event.code 7045, appear on nashua at the same times), i.e. lateral movement/remote admin, not interception of MFA tokens. No smart-card, PKINIT, or MFA-provider fields are present.

findings.title: RDP logons (LogonType 10) for pbeesly use Negotiate, no smart-card/MFA provider
findings.summary: The only LogonType 10 (RemoteInteractive) successful logons are two events on scranton.dmevals.local for user pbeesly from 172.18.39.2, authenticated with AuthenticationPackageName 'Negotiate' and LogonProcessName 'User32'. There is no Kerberos PKINIT, smart-card, or MFA/credential-provider indication, so these are ordinary RDP sessions rather than intercepted MFA authentication.

findings.title: Credential-related registry writes are built-in Windows components (Credential Guard disabled, CredentialEnrollmentManager service)
findings.summary: The 11 Sysmon event.code 13 registry writes matching 'Credential' are all legitimate Windows internals: lsass.exe setting HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to DWORD (0x00000000) (Credential Guard is disabled — a defensive-posture observation, not interception), and services.exe registering the built-in CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service (ImagePath C:\windows\system32\CredentialEnrollmentManager.exe) plus MuiCache entries. No attacker-controlled credential-provider DLL or vault tampering is present.

findings.title: No smart-card, MFA, token, vault or credential-provider artifacts observed
findings.summary: Targeted hunts for MFA-interception indicators returned nothing: no Sysmon process-creation (event.code 1) with smartcard/scard/MFA/token in the command line, no file-creation (event.code 11) touching Credential/smartcard/scard paths, no vaultcmd/CredentialEnrollmentManager process execution, and no PowerShell script-block (4104) referencing Credential. The only 'Credential' text in windows.other is a benign 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' message. There is no evidence of MFA token interception on any host.

On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on ports 445 and 139; every attempt was rejected (conn_state REJ, 0 bytes), showing the target does not run SMB. The client then fell back to WebDAV over HTTP port 80: a DavClnt OPTIONS to '/' returned 403, followed by Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 OPTIONS and PROPFIND requests to /webdav, /webdav/ and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The first PROPFIND request carried an AUTHORIZATION header (client_header_names includes AUTHORIZATION) and the server answered 401 Unauthorized on the OfficeSupplies.7z path, i.e. the victim's credentials were transmitted to the attacker-controlled WebDAV listener. This is the classic forced-authentication chain (SCF/URL file or UNC path pointing at a WebDAV share) used to capture NTLM hashes. The activity is confined to the zeek window (2020-04-30) which does not overlap the Windows host logs (2020-05-02).
findings.title: WebDAV forced-authentication (NTLM leak) from scranton to attacker host 192.168.0.4

findings.summary: The 163 share-access events (5140/5145) on newyork.dmevals.local are SYSVOL, IPC$ and ADMIN$ accesses by domain computer accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$, WEC$) and by user pbeesly, sourced from the internal 10.0.1.x range and link-local IPv6. These are routine domain logon-script, GPO and admin-share operations, not forced authentication: the accounts are the machines' own computer accounts and the shares are the standard AD shares. No attacker-controlled listener or credential-capture pattern is present in this dataset.
findings.title: Inbound SMB share access (SYSVOL/IPC$/ADMIN$) is normal domain machine-account traffic

findings.summary: Sysmon event 3 shows 66 outbound SMB connections, all from the System process (PID 4) on the domain hosts, with destinations 10.0.0.4 (newyork, the DC) and 10.0.1.6, plus link-local IPv6 self-connections. Zeek conn records for 445/139 are dominated by 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 and 10.0.0.4. These are normal domain controller / SYSVOL replication and machine-account authentication flows within the internal network, not connections to an external or attacker-controlled SMB listener. The only anomalous SMB destination (192.168.0.4) was rejected and is captured in the malicious WebDAV finding above.
findings.title: Outbound SMB (445/139) from workstations is internal domain traffic, not attacker listeners

findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF on scranton.dmevals.local. This is the canonical signature of in-memory credential dumping (e.g. MiniDumpWriteDump / reflective loader). It coincides with a PowerShell script block that builds a reflective shellcode loader (GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle/ReflectedDelegate + base64 shellcode), and with keystroke-logging, screen-capture and clipboard-theft activity on the same host — consistent with an adversary exploiting/abusing the host to steal credentials.

findings.title: WinRM host process (wsmprovhost.exe) accessed LSASS with 0x1F3FFF on nashua.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:09:29, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the WinRM remote-shell host, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF on nashua.dmevals.local. The call trace shows PowerShell command-management assemblies, i.e. a remote PowerShell session reading LSASS memory. Immediately after, the same session enumerated processes with usernames and collected/archived credential-related files (pass/login/admin/vpn patterns) into working.zip — consistent with credential access via a remotely-driven exploitation/abuse of the host.

No anomalous encryption downgrade, no RC4/kerberoasting pattern, no unusual service names — consistent with normal domain authentication, not exploitation for credential access.

findings.title: Zeek weird/notice records are protocol anomalies, not exploitation
findings.summary: The 14 Zeek notice/weird records on 2020-04-30 are generic network anomalies: ip_hdr_len_zero, truncated_IP, unknown_dce_rpc_auth_type (addl 68) between 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 and 10.0.0.4, and self-signed SSL certificate validation failures. These are common malformed-packet/self-signed-cert artifacts with no exploit payload, no CVE signature and no credential-access content. They also fall in a time window (2020-04-30) that does not overlap the Windows credential-access activity (2020-05-02).

findings.title: WebDAV DavSetCookie activity on scranton.dmevals.local is a WebDAV client cookie, not browser session cookie theft
findings.summary: Five 4688 process-creation events on scranton.dmevals.local (2020-05-01 23:08:50 and 23:10:22-23) show rundll32.exe invoking davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie against 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav, spawned by svchost.exe under user pbeesly. DavSetCookie is the WebDAV redirector's own cookie mechanism for a WebDAV mount, not theft of a browser/web-application session cookie. The same command line also appears in Sysmon event.code 1. No browser cookie store was touched.

findings.title: INetCookies file creation by svchost.exe is a Windows service-profile artifact, not cookie theft
findings.summary: The only Sysmon file-creation event matching *cookie* is svchost.exe (PID 7200, SYSTEM) creating C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-...\AC\INetCookies on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02 03:21:05. This is a Windows WARP JIT service package artifact under the LocalService profile, not a browser cookie database (no Chrome/Edge/Firefox Cookies, Login Data or Web Data files were created or accessed anywhere in the dataset).

findings.title: Zeek HTTP GET /webdav/python.exe reflects WebDAV payload retrieval, not session-cookie use
findings.summary: The two Zeek HTTP GET hits (2020-04-30 00:35:25, observer simplerockbuild.simplerock.lan, 10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.4:80) are Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir requests for /webdav/python.exe returning 401 Unauthorized. They carry no Cookie header and represent WebDAV file retrieval (consistent with the python.exe dropped to C:\Windows\Temp on nashua.dmevals.local), not web session cookie theft. Zeek's window does not overlap the Windows host logs.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script (loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 / psversion.ps1) defining Get-PrivateKeys, which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and exports every certificate with a thumbprint to a randomly-named .pfx in the user's Downloads folder, protected by the hardcoded password "saribas". This is direct private-key/certificate theft (T1552.004).

findings.title: Hardcoded credentials in PowerShell scripts and PsExec command line

The same host's PowerShell scripts also embed plaintext credentials (Invoke-Exfil uses $Password = "MyCozyPassw0rd!" and a 7-Zip archive password "lolol"). These are credentials-in-files/command-line exposures used to move laterally.
